mcqs.question: A team says "we need NoSQL because our relational database is too slow." What's the strongest follow-up question?
options: Which of scale, flexible schema, or developer velocity is actually the driver — and can you show the specific bottleneck?
Which NoSQL vendor does your team prefer?
Have you considered switching cloud providers instead?
Is your team willing to rewrite the entire application?
mcqs.explanation: Naming the actual driver forces a concrete diagnosis instead of a vague performance complaint, which often turns out to be a missing index or bad query, not a database-family problem. Vendor preference, cloud provider, and a rewrite are downstream decisions that shouldn't come before diagnosing the real cause.

mcqs.question: A fraud-detection system needs to find rings of connected accounts through multiple hops of shared devices, IPs, and payment methods. Which NoSQL family fits best?
options: Key-value — fastest raw lookup speed
Document — flexible schema for varying account attributes
Wide-column — highest write throughput
Graph — built for multi-hop relationship traversal queries
mcqs.explanation: Multi-hop relationship traversal is exactly what graph databases are optimized for, using nodes and edges instead of repeated joins. Key-value and document don't model relationships natively, and wide-column's strength is write throughput, not traversal.

mcqs.question: A team skips data-model planning because "our document store is schemaless." What actually happens to the schema?
options: There genuinely is no schema and nothing needs to be planned
The schema is enforced by the database automatically regardless of planning
The schema still exists but shifts to being enforced by application code at read time instead of the database at write time
The database rejects any document that doesn't match the first one written
mcqs.explanation: Schema-on-read means the structure still exists conceptually — it just isn't validated until application code reads the data, so inconsistent shapes can silently accumulate. The database doesn't auto-enforce or reject anything in a schemaless store, and "no schema at all" is the actual misconception being corrected.

mcqs.question: A team's data is genuinely relational — orders reference customers who share addresses — but they pick a document database to avoid writing joins. What's the likely consequence?
options: The relational structure disappears once the data model changes
Nothing changes; document databases handle relational data identically to relational databases
Performance always improves because document databases are inherently faster
The relational structure moves into application code, which now must fetch related documents across multiple round trips and keep denormalized copies consistent by hand
mcqs.explanation: The underlying relationships don't vanish just because the database changed — the application now has to do by hand what a relational engine's join logic did for it. Document stores don't handle genuinely relational data the same way, and switching databases doesn't guarantee a performance gain.

mcqs.question: A banking feature needs to atomically debit one account and credit another. Why would most NoSQL stores be a weaker fit than a relational database here?
options: NoSQL databases cannot store monetary values accurately
Multi-row/multi-document atomic transactions are native to relational ACID engines, while many NoSQL stores lack them or added them with real performance cost
NoSQL databases are always slower for any single write
Relational databases are the only databases that support currency data types
mcqs.explanation: Relational engines are built around multi-row ACID transactions as a core feature; many NoSQL stores either don't support multi-document transactions or added them later at real performance cost. Monetary storage and currency types aren't the distinguishing factor, and NoSQL isn't universally slower for single writes.

mcqs.question: A team assumes they need a wide-column NoSQL store because "a single database can't handle our write volume." Their actual measured peak is 3,000 writes/sec. What should they check first?
options: Whether a well-tuned single relational primary (often sustaining 5,000-20,000 writes/sec) can already handle this load before adopting a more complex system
Which cloud region has the lowest network latency
Whether their NoSQL vendor offers a free tier
How many total tables their schema currently has
mcqs.explanation: A well-tuned relational primary can often sustain far more than 3,000 writes/sec, so the actual number should be checked against realistic relational throughput before adding NoSQL's complexity. Region latency, vendor pricing, and table count don't address whether the scale claim is even true.
